What then will an inexperienced shepherd be able to answer to the charges, he who was negligent in the care of the sheep? He must fall silent, because he has nothing to answer. Therefore, brother, if you consider yourself fit for the care of souls, if you are preparing to govern the church of Mernicensem, know that you are to be brought into judgment for these things, and according to the merit of your life will receive either glory or torment. But believe me, he dies secure who, leaving aside concern for others, lives for himself alone in the fear of God. For to whom much is entrusted, much also will be required from him. A priest, especially one having the care of souls, is God’s herald, to announce to the people the will of the Almighty and to heal sinners in the law of the Lord by words of rebuke. Therefore he must be learned and most steadfast, lest he either slip through ignorance or through inconstancy fear the hatred of the perverse. It is shameful

For it is, through fear of the people, to keep silent the words of God. A priest must make use of wine sparingly, lest, if he gives himself over to drinking bouts, he become a reproach among the people. For the Apostle condemns wine-bibbing priests, and the old law forbids them access to the altar. In the Council of Agde also it is read thus: Before all things drunkenness is to be avoided by clerics, for it is the tinder and nurse of all vices. And so he who is found to have been drunk, as his rank allows, is either to be removed from communion for the space of thirty days, or subjected to bodily punishment. For wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness brings reproach; everyone who is mingled with these will not be wise. He who burns without wine, with the heat of youth, and is inflamed by the warmth of the blood, and is of vigorous body, should flee wine as poison, lest, suffocated by a manifold conflagration, he fall into the filth of lust.

A stomach heated with wine stirs up desire, dulls the senses, and weakens the head and the whole body. A fat belly begets a thin understanding. Therefore, when you go as an invited guest to banquets of priests, do not forget clerical honor, but show yourself modest and restrained in all things; and take care that neither your tongue nor your itching ears, that is, that neither you yourself detract from others, nor lend your hearing to those who detract. Know that everything you say about others is to be turned back upon yourself, and perhaps you will be found guilty in the very things that you were reproving in others. But perhaps you will say: I cannot do injury to those who report it, for anyone strives in vain who plans to stop the lips of all. What, then, is another's detraction to me? Surely I cannot forbid men to speak? But, as we said above, so present yourself before the detractor that he may learn to detract from no one, when he sees that you do not willingly hear what is being said. Solomon says: Do not associate with detractors, for their destruction will come suddenly. And who knows the ruin of both: of him, that is, who detracts, and of him who lends his ear to the detractor? Be mature in morals and manner of life, sparing and prudent in words, discreet in silence and taciturnity. Be diligent in investigating the mysteries of the Scriptures; and if anything doubtful occurs to you as you read, know that it must be referred to the interpretations of the elders. You have nearby an ancient

of the most ancient city of Trier, a school in which there is an abundance of learned men; to them, when questions are doubtful, you will be able to have recourse. Let gold not be dearer to you than knowledge, for the fruit of wisdom is eternal, but the use of riches is brief and momentary. Let there be no one who prevents salutary study: not mother, not brother, not sister. You, do the work of an evangelist; learn what you are to teach, lest you turn out to be a shepherd and an idol. You are one, and have no second: for whom, then, would you store up riches? Live temperately; do not frequent weddings and immoderate banquets, for they both strip the mind of virtues and render the purse empty of coins. Procure for yourself, from the alms offered, copies of divine Scripture, by whose constant reading, made learned, you may worthily instruct the people committed to you, and raise your own self by contemplation to heavenly things. Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and it will exalt you before God and men. Do not consent to the pleasures of the flesh; restrain the impulse of fury; and never forget death.
What sort the priest ought to be in his inner conduct. Chapter 7.

Since, however, it is not enough for a minister of Christ to lead honorable conduct before men, unless he also strives to appear pure from every crime before God, I exhort you to direct your heart in the fear of the Almighty, and never admit any thoughts against God. For the priest of God must be holy in mind and body, and pure in thought. Hence the Lord says: Be holy, for I am holy, the Lord your God, who sanctify you. And Peter, the chief apostle, says: You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. Let charity hold the first place in your heart, for it is the fullness of the law and the completion of the prophets. For the greatest of all virtues is charity, which consists in love of God and neighbor.

Chapter 6.

God, however, is to be loved with the whole heart for his own sake, and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. No one truly loves God if he [unclear] hates his neighbor. For Christ is God and man. Therefore whoever hates man hates the whole Christ. God accepts no good work unless the flame of charity kindles it upon the altar of the heart. For charity holds the chief place among all the virtues. Humility follows it, which is remembered as the guardian of the virtues. So great is the eminence of this virtue that every other one quickly perishes unless it is strengthened on the foundation of humility. Saint Pope Gregory says: He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind. From the place where he is seen to carry something, there he is the more gravely blinded.

Therefore the greatest adornment of a priest is charity, and the most precious pearl in that splendid garment is humility. You too, brother, display these twin virtues in yourself, and you will be a fruitful preacher in the church of God. Whatever you say you will easily persuade your hearers, if you have charity and humility in your heart and diligently show them in your work. Let cursed ambition have no place in your heart; once it has invaded the mind, it so blinds it that it brings forgetfulness of God’s saving [unclear]. Be a Christian lover of men and an enemy of vices. Keep the commandments of God, and neglect none of the ecclesiastical sanctions. Honor all men for God’s sake, and judge no one at all to be despised. What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. Let not the sun set upon your anger. Flee the flatteries of the rich, and never caress sinners. Deny your rash desires, so that you may become a disciple of Christ. Chastise your body, according to the apostle, bringing it back into servitude; despise delights; love chaste fasting. Be kind to the poor: feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, free the captive, console the sorrowful, bury the dead. Love nothing in the world; seek no riches; run after no vanity. For no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs. Do injury to no one, but learn to bear patiently what is inflicted, after the example of God, who, hanging on the cross, [prayed?] for his persecutors that they should not perish. Have peace with all men, but concord and unanimity only with the devout.

Do not be proud and arrogant, not sleepy and lazy, not given to wine and much eating, not a detractor and one who rashly judges anyone. Guard your actions at every hour, and let the memory of the things to come always turn in your thought. For Scripture says: Son, remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. Accordingly always think that you are going to die; fear the day of judgment; dread the torments of hell. If you do these things, you will easily overcome all temptations of the flesh. Despise the pleasures of the world, so that you may be able to enter rejoicing into the joys of heavenly happiness. Do not deceive your soul: no one can rejoice here with the world and afterward reign with Christ. For through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. Therefore, with present things despised, let us hasten with all desire toward eternal joys. With all watchfulness guard your heart, since life proceeds from it. If you have been overtaken by some offense, do not delay in seeking the remedies of penitence, and in cleansing yourself in confession through true contrition. Strive to enter by the narrow way into life: that is, not to fulfill the desires of the flesh, to hate the world, to live in the spirit. You have been called to serve God as a soldier against the vices of the flesh; do not rest before victory, do not cease from the battle, for no one will be crowned unless he is victor. In this life, however, there is no certain victory, but continual battle. He who perseveres to the end will be saved. A man will be approved at his end. The life of man upon earth is warfare. For as a soldier of the highest king, it is not permitted you to abandon his contest. A good soldier follows his king wherever he goes. Where, then, is your king? In heaven. Why do you not follow him? What are you doing on earth, if you are a soldier of the heavenly king above? Why do you not follow your lord? He himself says: He who ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also my minister will be. Let him follow, he says, not with the steps of feet, but with the steps of affections. The apostle also says: No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has approved himself. Therefore, just as those who serve an earthly king obey all his commands, and wherever they are sent are ready and prompt,

excusing themselves on account of wife or children: so it is fitting for the soldier of Christ to obey his commands in all things, and in nothing at all to excuse himself. You therefore, who await the unfading crown of victory, toil like a good soldier of Jesus Christ: let no care of earthly anxiety weigh you down; let no enticement of fleshly pleasure touch your mind. For nothing is happier than the soldier of Christ, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised; nothing more toilsome, than one who daily runs risk of his life; nothing stronger, than one who conquers the devil; nothing weaker, than one who is overcome by the flesh. Let not home draw you away; let not kinship hinder you; let not the flesh constrain you. I wish you to be without anxiety, so that you may freely think on the things that are God’s. Naked and unencumbered fly to heaven, because naked your mother bore you, and naked the earth will receive you. Love what you cannot [unclear]; seek where you may rejoice happily for eternity. Live so that you do not fear to die. A good conscience does not fear death, because through it it knows that it will come to the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland. You now have, most beloved brother, what you asked of me; you have a certain pattern of good conduct on which you may imprint yourself; you have a rule of holy exhortation to which you may diligently have recourse. I have done what I could, not as much as I wished. For the rest, live according to the Gospel and the constitutions of the holy fathers, in which the whole form of Christian perfection is seen. Farewell, mindful of us. From Sponheim, on the Kalends of April, in the year 1486. Here ends the little book of lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, On the Life of Priests.
